issues.legal_issue: A dying declaration recorded by a police officer may be admitted and relied on as the sole basis for conviction when it is reliable, voluntary, and made by a person fit to give a statement.
material_facts: The injured declarant gave a statement in hospital identifying the assailants and describing their actions.
A doctor certified that she was mentally fit to make a statement, and she signed it after it was recorded.
The statement was clear and consistent, and medical evidence showed that she could speak despite her injuries.
The declaration was recorded by an investigating officer rather than a Magistrate; the officer’s account was not materially shaken in cross-examination.
The trial and appellate courts found the declaration credible, and the Supreme Court found no reason to reject it.
issues.conclusion: The police-recorded dying declaration was admissible and sufficiently reliable to sustain conviction without corroboration; the absence of a Magistrate’s recording did not by itself invalidate it.
issues.legal_principle: A dying declaration can alone sustain conviction if, after careful scrutiny, the court is satisfied that it is true, voluntary, coherent, and made by a person in a fit state of mind; corroboration is a rule of prudence, not an absolute requirement. A declaration recorded by a police officer is not automatically inadmissible merely because a Magistrate did not record it. The Court relied on Munnu Raja v. State of Madhya Pradesh, Paras Yadav v. State of Bihar, Balbir Singh v. State of Punjab, State of Karnataka v. Shariff, Ram Bihari Yadav v. State of Bihar, Laxman v. State of Maharashtra, State of Rajasthan v. Wakteng, Bijoy Das v. State of West Bengal, Muthu Kutty v. State, Panneerselvam v. State of Tamil Nadu, and Paniben v. State of Gujarat.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_challenging_conviction and conviction_relies_on_dying_declaration and declaration_recorded_by_police and declarant_medically_fit and declaration_clear_and_consistent and declaration_voluntary and not material_infirmity

predicates.criminal_appeal_challenging_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.conviction_relies_on_dying_declaration: The conviction rests on a statement made by a person who later died.
predicates.declaration_recorded_by_police: A police officer recorded the declarant’s statement.
predicates.declarant_medically_fit: Medical evidence or certification indicated that the declarant was fit to make a statement.
predicates.declaration_clear_and_consistent: The declarant gave a coherent account that was not materially contradictory.
predicates.declaration_voluntary: The evidence supported that the declarant spoke freely and was not tutored or prompted.
predicates.material_infirmity: The declaration had a material defect, such as evidence that the declarant was unconscious or unable to make a statement.

issues.definition: When a criminal appeal challenges a conviction based on a police-recorded dying declaration, a fit declarant’s clear, consistent, and voluntary statement without material infirmity may support conviction on its own.

issues.legal_issue: The death penalty is appropriate only in the rarest of rare cases after the aggravating and mitigating circumstances relating to both the crime and the offender have been balanced.
material_facts: The principal offender planned the killings to obtain control of family property before his father’s death.
He killed three members of the family, including young and helpless victims, after the victims were confined inside the house.
He inflicted numerous knife injuries on the victims, and the Court characterized the killings as exceptionally brutal and deliberate.
The offender was 25 years old and had no prior criminal history; the Court considered these and other mitigating submissions but found them outweighed by the circumstances of the crime.
The other convicted participant received life imprisonment, and that sentence was also confirmed.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the principal offender’s crimes were of extreme culpability and fell within the rarest of rare category, so it confirmed the death sentence; it also confirmed the life sentence imposed on the other convicted participant.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and Section 354(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, life imprisonment is the rule and death is the exception. The court must consider circumstances of both the crime and the offender, give full weight to mitigating circumstances, and impose death only where life imprisonment is inadequate and no alternative can be conscientiously chosen. The Court applied Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab and the categories and guidance in Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab, including consideration of planning, brutality, motive, magnitude of the crime, victims’ vulnerability, and mitigating circumstances.

rule.if: capital_sentence_appeal and offender_planned_killings and multiple_victims and extreme_brutality and property_gain_motive and victims_were_helpless and offender_was_young_without_prior_record

predicates.capital_sentence_appeal: The proceeding asks an appellate court to review a death sentence.
predicates.offender_planned_killings: The offender planned the killings before carrying them out.
predicates.multiple_victims: The crime involved the killing of multiple people.
predicates.extreme_brutality: The offender carried out the killings with exceptional brutality.
predicates.property_gain_motive: The offender committed the killings to obtain control of property.
predicates.victims_were_helpless: The victims were unarmed or otherwise unable to resist or escape.
predicates.offender_was_young_without_prior_record: The offender was young and had no prior criminal history.

issues.definition: In an appeal reviewing a death sentence, planned property-motivated killings of multiple helpless victims with exceptional brutality may warrant death even where the offender was young and had no prior criminal history.
